Ravi to share benchmark config and propose batching/caching settings
Schedule technical deep dive with Elysian infra team next week

summary: Discovery focused on unit economics for hosted vs dedicated vs private deployments. Elysian wants clear per-token cost, impact of batching and KV/prefix caching, and estimate for commit vs pay-as-you-go. Main constraints: strict data residency for some models, budget target ~$25k/mo for initial phase, and desire for predictable latency under 250ms p50.
topics: pricing SKUs, per-token economics, batching and caching levers, dedicated capacity vs hosted, private/VPC constraints, SOC2/KMS, pilot timeline and success criteria
transcript:
Header: 2026-03-04 14:00 EDT | Duration 45m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Sofia Alvarez (Head of ML, Elysian), David Kim (Infra Lead), Liam O'Neill (CTO)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Ravi our solutions engineer. quick check audio?
[00:08] Sofia: hi yep all good, thanks Maya.
[00:12] Liam: good to go.
[00:15] Maya: Awesome. Today's agenda is quick discovery on cost per token and how batching/caching can move the needle, plus figure out whether hosted, dedicated, or private makes sense for your footprint. Sound right?
[00:27] David: Yep perfect. we're primarily evaluating for our research assistants and trade desk helpers, so cost matters a lot.
[00:34] Ravi: Great. could you share current stack and volumes? rough numbers are fine.
[00:39] Sofia: yeah so we have about 200k tokens/day avg across prod and stage, spikes to like 1.5M on market open. latency target p50 under 250ms, p95 under 800ms. Right now we're using openapi access to some public provider but costs are spiking and tail latency is inconsistent.
[00:57] Maya: got it. budget wise any targets?
[01:00] Liam: for the pilot we want to keep under $25k/month total. long term could scale but want predictable unit costs first.
[01:09] Ravi: ok that's helpful. just to calibrate: Redwood hosted pricing is per-token plus options for committed capacity which lowers unit price; dedicated sits between hosted and private in cost/latency tradeoff, private adds overhead for infra and ops but gives isolation.
[01:26] Sofia: can you quantify per-token? even ballpark?
[01:29] Maya: sure, for the models you mentioned historically ballpark gzipped tokens, but to keep it simple: hosted pay-as-you-go for our mid-size models is roughly $0.0005 to $0.001 per input token depending on model and output length. committed/dedicated can drop that 20-50% depending on commit tier and batching.
[01:46] David: when you say batching, is that automatic? how much does it actually help our use case with low latency requirements?
[01:52] Ravi: important question. Redwood supports continuous batching in the runtime — the system will batch compatible requests at sub-100ms windows when latency SLOs allow. For chat-style short requests, benefits are modest maybe 10-30% cost reduction. For long completion workloads or high qps bursts, batching can reduce cost 40%+ because of kernel amortization. prefix/KV caching helps for repeated prompts — that can be another 20-60% savings if you have repeated prefixes.
[02:19] Sofia: our assistants reuse a lot of context and system prompts, so KV cache sounds promising. any constraints on recall or freshness?
[02:25] Ravi: KV cache is per-model and we support invalidation policies; it's best for static system and few-shot prompts. if you need highly dynamic user-specific state, cache hit rates drop. We'll need sample traffic to estimate hit rate.
[02:37] Liam: regarding latency, would dedicated guarantee p95 under 800ms?
[02:41] Maya: our dedicated SKU offers SLA-backed latency targets and reserved GPU pools; typical p50 for many models on dedicated with optimized kernels is sub-200ms for short sequences. p95 depends on sequence length and concurrency but dedicated plus autoscale/burst gives much more predictability during market open spikes.
[02:59] David: we have data residency needs for trade desk — can you do VPC or on-prem?
[03:04] Maya: yes Redwood Private provides a customer VPC control plane or full on-prem option. that adds integration overhead and a platform fee but solves residency and key management — we integrate with customer KMS/HSM.
[03:15] Sofia: ok good. can you walk through an example of cost math for 1M tokens/day with 30% batching and 25% cache hit?
[03:23] Ravi: quick calc: raw tokens 1M/day -> 30M/mo. baseline hosted payg at $0.0008/token avg -> $24k/mo. With 30% batching improvement reduce compute to ~0.7x -> ~ $16.8k. With 25% cache hit saving another 25% on the cached portion roughly -> effective further reduction ~ $13k. if you commit to dedicated at a 30% discount vs hosted you might land around $9-10k but plus base reserved capacity cost. these are illustrative; we'll run the spreadsheet.
[04:04] Liam: interesting, those numbers move a lot. but committed means a monthly bill even if traffic dips, right?
[04:09] Maya: correct; committed buys lower per-unit pricing and reserved throughput. we usually model a 3-12 month commit with step-down tiers. We can show a hybrid: committed baseline for steady traffic plus burst on hosted.
[04:21] David: what about quantization / model variants? can that reduce cost further without losing accuracy?
[04:25] Ravi: yes model quantization and smaller model variants can reduce GPU cycles. Our Optimize tooling recommends quantization profiles per workload; e.g., moving from fp16 to int8 quantized runtime can give 1.5-2x throughput improvements and lower per-token cost. We recommend running evals on your prompts to measure quality impact.
[04:40] Sofia: we are sensitive to hallucinations so can't drop quality too much. how do you surface regression risks?
[04:45] Maya: we have eval hooks and quality monitoring; you can tie alerts to prompt sets and get regression diffs. we can include that in the pilot scope.
[04:52] Liam: security — do you retain customer data on hosted? encryption at rest?
[04:56] Maya: hosted can be configured to not persist user data, and we support encrypted-at-rest with customer-managed keys in dedicated/private. audit logs and RBAC available. we'll send SOC2 and network diagrams.
[05:06] David: ok good. one more on cost: how are tokens counted for mixed input/output? like we do short prompts but long generated summaries sometimes 400-600 tokens.
[05:16] Ravi: billing counts both input and output tokens; the per-token effective price changes with sequence length because longer outputs get amortized across kernel setup but also cost more raw tokens. In the spreadsheet we'll model distribution of input/output lengths to get accurate monthly spend.
[05:28] Sofia: for our pilot, we can provide a week of logs showing token lengths and qps.
[05:33] Maya: perfect — that's exactly what Ravi needs to model commit tiers and caching gains.
[05:37] Liam: timeline — we'd like pilot next quarter, two week pilot followed by decision window of 4 weeks.
[05:43] Maya: sounds reasonable. success criteria?
[05:46] Sofia: stay under $25k/month with p50 latency <250ms and no data egress outside our region.
[05:52] Ravi: noted. Also to confirm, are there any legal/procurement blockers?
[05:56] Liam: standard NDAs ok; main is review of SOC2 and contracts. procurement typically needs 30 days to review.
[06:03] Maya: we'll attach SOC2 report and standard entitlements.
[06:06] David: question — on batching windows, do you expose control to tune latency vs batch size?
[06:11] Ravi: yes you can set latency SLOs and batching thresholds; runtime will opportunistically batch within those windows. We'll recommend defaults but you can override per-route.
[06:20] Sofia: nice. about KV cache — any limits on size or eviction?
[06:24] Ravi: current limits depend on deployment; hosted has TTL and eviction policies, dedicated/private allow larger in-memory caches and custom eviction. we'll outline config options in the follow-up.
[06:35] Liam: competitors — are you seeing customers move away from OpenAI for cost reasons?
[06:39] Maya: yes some customers are shifting part of workloads to open models on Redwood to reduce cost and improve control. others keep a hybrid where LLMs with strict quality use commercial models.
[06:48] David: ok that's helpful.
[06:50] Maya: wrapping up next steps: I'll send pricing SKUs + commit worksheet, Ravi will run a benchmark config once you share logs, and we'll schedule a technical deep dive. Anything else?
[07:02] Sofia: please include example invoice line items so procurement can see monthly cadence.
[07:06] Maya: Will do. thanks all.
[07:09] Liam: thanks.
[07:11] End transcript (call lasted approx 45 minutes).
